enonce_markdown: Other things being equal, a rise in the rate of interest will cause the quantity of investment demanded to
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Investment demand (the marginal efficiency of capital schedule) slopes downward: fewer projects have an expected return above a higher cost of borrowing.

### Solution

A higher interest rate raises the cost of borrowing and the opportunity cost of using own funds, so projects whose expected yield is below the new rate are dropped. Investment **falls**, a movement up along the downward-sloping investment demand curve. **Answer: a.**

enonce_markdown: In a year, net investment in an economy is 380 billion FCFA and depreciation of the capital stock is 120 billion FCFA. Gross investment is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Gross investment = net investment + depreciation (replacement investment).

### Solution

Gross investment $= 380 + 120 = 500$ billion FCFA. 260 comes from subtracting depreciation, and 380 is net investment only. **Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown: A firm can buy a machine for 20,000,000 FCFA that will add 2,400,000 FCFA a year to its net revenue. The firm will find the project profitable only if the rate of interest is below
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A firm compares the expected rate of return (marginal efficiency of capital) with the rate of interest: it invests if the expected return is greater than the cost of borrowing.

### Solution

Expected rate of return $= \dfrac{2{,}400{,}000}{20{,}000{,}000} \times 100 = 12\%$. The project is profitable only if the interest rate is below **12%**. The figure of 8.3% comes from inverting the ratio (20 / 2.4) and 24% from an arithmetic slip with the zeros. **Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown:
In an economy the capital-output ratio is 3 (3 units of capital are needed for each extra unit of annual output). National output rises by 200 billion FCFA in year 1 and by 100 billion FCFA in year 2.

(a) Calculate net investment in each year using the accelerator.

(b) Explain what happens to investment in year 2 although output is still rising.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The accelerator links **net investment** to the **change** in output: $I_{net} = v \times \Delta Y$, where $v$ is the capital-output ratio.

### Solution

(a) Year 1: $I = 3 \times 200 = 600$ billion FCFA. Year 2: $I = 3 \times 100 = 300$ billion FCFA.

(b) Output is still growing, but the **rate of increase** has halved, so net investment falls by half (600 to 300). Investment depends on the change in output, not its level, so it is volatile: a slowdown in growth can reduce investment and, through lower incomes, reduce demand further.

enonce_markdown: Which of the following is most likely to shift the investment demand curve to the **right**?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A shift of the curve is caused by a change in a determinant other than the interest rate (expected profit, taxes, costs of capital goods). A change in the interest rate itself is a movement along the curve.

### Solution

Improved expectations of future sales raise the expected return on every project, so more investment is demanded at each rate of interest: the curve shifts right. A fall in the interest rate (a) is a movement along the curve; a higher company tax (b) and higher import duties on machinery (c) lower the net return, shifting it left. **Answer: d.**

choix.texte: A fall in the rate of interest
A rise in the rate of company tax
A rise in import duties on machinery
Firms become more optimistic about future sales

enonce_markdown: During a recession the central bank cuts the interest rate from 8% to 6%, but private investment hardly changes. The most likely explanation is that
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Interest affects investment by moving along the investment demand curve, but expectations shift the curve. If the shift offsets the interest cut, quantity demanded may not change.

### Solution

Pessimistic expectations about future sales cut the expected return on projects at every interest rate, shifting the investment demand curve left. The lower rate moves firms down along the curve, but the leftward shift offsets it, so investment barely changes. Interest rates do affect investment (b is false), the accelerator is not zero but depends on expected demand (c), and high savings (d) do not stop firms investing when credit is cheap. **Answer: a.**

choix.texte: pessimistic expectations have shifted the investment demand curve to the left, offsetting the effect of lower interest
the interest rate has no effect on investment
the accelerator is always zero in a recession
a high level of savings stops firms from borrowing
